extracted.intended_audience: gentlemen/courtiers seeking guidance on comportment at Renaissance courts
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and norms for the ideal courtier's conduct in public and private: how to perform at martial sports, music, dance, conversation, and in service to a prince. Emphasizes discretion, adaptation to occasion/age/rank, modesty in accepting favors, and limits of obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be fully equipped before public martial exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: When our Courtier has to take part in these, he must first contrive to be so well equipped in point of horses, weapons and dress, that he lacks nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not engage in jousts, tourneys or other martial displays unless you have the proper horses, weapons, and dress; failure cannot be excused as 'not my business.' If inadequately provided, abstain from participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the company and occasion before displaying feats
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully consider in whose presence he is seen and of what sort the company is, for it would not be seemly for a gentleman to honour a rustic festival with his presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match performance to the social context: avoid appearing at lowly festivals or before ignoble crowds where the display would be unseemly or lower one's dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only contest with inferiors as practice and courtesy, not rivalry
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever cares to wrestle or run or leap with peasants, ought to do so as a matter of practice and out of courtesy…a man ought to be almost sure of winning; else let him not engage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you take part in physical contests with lower-status participants, do so politely and for practice, not in competitive rivalry; avoid risking being vanquished (especially at wrestling) since that is shameful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice public sports but show indifference to praise
rubrics_metrics.description: I would have our Courtier practise this, and all the others...as something that is not his profession, and let him show that he does not seek or expect praise for it, nor let him seem to devote much care or time to it, although he may do it admirably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate skill (e.g., tennis, dancing) but display it with nonchalance; avoid giving the impression that accomplishments are your primary pursuit or that you seek applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentatious or constant public display
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not on earth a thing so excellent but the ignorant will tire of it and hold it of small account, if they see it often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit frequency of public performances; excessive visibility cheapens even notable talents. Seek selective, well-timed displays rather than constant showing-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve dignity in public dancing; temper grace with restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: When dancing in the presence of many...he should preserve a certain dignity, albeit tempered with a lithe and airy grace of movement...let him not attempt those agilities...which perhaps would be little suited to a gentleman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In public, dance with composed, graceful movements appropriate to rank; reserve more flamboyant or specialised steps for private settings (or masked occasions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use disguise selectively to enhance entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Disguise carries with it a certain freedom and licence...enable a man to choose a part for which he feels himself qualified, and to use care and elaboration upon the chief point of the thing wherein he would display himself, and a certain nonchalance as to that which does not count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In masked sports/shows, disguise allows creative roles and freer performance; choose parts that suit your abilities and concentrate effort on the principal effect while showing detached ease about lesser details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruler should avoid playing the ruler in masquerade
rubrics_metrics.description: It would not be seemly for a prince to try to enact the part of a prince, because that pleasure which the spectators find in novelty would be in great measure lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prince should avoid obvious self-portrayal in entertainments; better to lower rank overtly when mingling so merit, not authority, can shine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frequent public exposure in martial and athletic displays
rubrics_metrics.description: In horseback vaulting too, in wrestling, running and leaping, I should be well pleased to have him shun the vulgar crowd, or at most let himself be very rarely seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appear rarely at public athletic exhibitions to maintain distinction and prevent the ignorant from growing bored or contemptuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use music discreetly: as pastime, almost unwillingly, and judged by company
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the Courtier resort to music as a pastime and almost unwillingly, and not before vulgar people nor very many...hide the study and pains that are necessary in everything one would do well, and seem to value this accomplishment lightly in himself, but by practising it admirably make others value it highly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform music sparingly and in suitable company (preferably intimate and with ladies present). Conceal the labour behind skill; do not parade your study or solicit performance opportunities before large or vulgar crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer solo singing with viol or keyed/stringed instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: I regard as beautiful music, to sing well by note, with ease and in beautiful style; but as even far more beautiful, to sing to the accompaniment of the viol...All keyed instruments also are pleasing...not less charming is the music of the stringed quartet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate ability in solo voice with viol accompaniment and familiarity with keyed and stringed ensemble music—these are especially esteemed forms of music for a courtier to know.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right time for music: familiar, beloved company and ladies
rubrics_metrics.description: As to the time for enjoying these various kinds of music, I think it is whenever a man finds himself in familiar and beloved companionship...But above all it is fitting where ladies are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play or sing when the company is intimate and receptive; music is especially apt in the presence of ladies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt entertainments and comportment to age
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unseemly...to see a man of any quality, — old, hoary and toothless...playing on a viol and singing in the midst of a company of ladies...This then is the pleasure it is fitting old men should take in music. I say the like of dancing...we ought to give up these exercises before our age forces us to give them up against our will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select amusements suited to your stage of life: older men should avoid youthful displays (singing/dancing before ladies) and instead employ age-appropriate entertainments (storytelling, measured speech). Youth should temper levity with calm judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old men should employ prudence and mild, sportive humour in conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Old men ought to guard against much self-praise...and to be like oracles consulted of all men; and in telling what they know, they ought to have the grace to speak to the point and temper the gravity of their years with a certain mild and sportive humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experience to speak concisely and pleasantly; avoid garrulousness, querulousness or officious scolding when entertaining or advising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Youth should correct natural faults and cultivate calm, reserved manner
rubrics_metrics.description: I greatly like to see a youth...who is master of himself, without those restless manners which are often seen at that age; because such youths seem to have a certain something in them above the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young men should temper impulsiveness and volubility: practice self-control, deliberateness, and a composed presence—particularly in martial contexts—since quietness can imply courageous judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a gentle and amiable manner in daily talk; adapt to interlocutor
rubrics_metrics.description: Not even all these qualities...will suffice...unless he has also a gentle and amiable manner in daily talk...must daily change his style and method according to the character of the person with whom he has to converse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be adaptable in conversation: vary tone and topics to suit interlocutors, exercising good judgment rather than fixed rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve the prince's tastes without becoming a flatterer
rubrics_metrics.description: I would have the Courtier strive...to love and almost to adore the prince whom he serves, and mould his wishes, habits and all his ways to his prince's liking...it is possible without flattery to obey and further the wishes of him we serve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to the prince's reasonable preferences and present agreeable conversation and habits; do so sincerely and respectfully, not by sycophantic flattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid negative courtly vices (flattery, tattling, obstinacy, evil-speaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: He will not be a bearer of evil tidings; he will not be thoughtless in sometimes saying things that offend instead of pleasing...He will not be an idle or untruthful tattler, nor a boaster nor pointless flatterer, but modest and reserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from gossip, slander, pointless contradiction, boastfulness and baseless flattery. Maintain modesty, reserve, and public reverence toward superiors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request favors seldom and with discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: He will very rarely or almost never ask anything of his lord for himself, lest his lord...grant it with an ill grace...Even in asking for others he will choose his time discreetly and ask proper and reasonable things; and he will so frame his request...that his lord shall always grant it, or shall not think him offended by refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid frequent or selfish petitions; when asking, choose an appropriate moment, frame requests to minimize displeasure, and accept refusals without apparent offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not intrude unasked into master's private retreats; alter manner when private
rubrics_metrics.description: He will not seek to intrude unasked into his master's chamber or private retreats...But if a Courtier...finds himself in private with his lord, he must put on another face, postpone grave concerns...and give the conversation a cast that shall amuse and please his lord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect a ruler's private space; when privately received, adapt to the lord's mood—avoid heavy matters unless appropriate and aim to amuse/relax rather than disturb repose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid greed and envy; be composed in favor or disfavour
rubrics_metrics.description: Let him above all take care not to weary his lord...do not angle for favours...if they happen to meet any disfavour or to see others favoured, they suffer such anguish that they can in no wise hide their envy...if they find themselves in at all more than common favour, they become so intoxicated by it that they stand palsied with joy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceal envy when others are favored and maintain composure when fortunate; excessive eagerness or visible envy damages reputation and can provoke spite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept favors modestly to increase donor's esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: A man ought always to be a little more backward than his rank warrants; to accept not too readily the favours and honours that are offered him; and to refuse them modestly, showing that he values them highly...the greater the reluctance...the more highly will the prince...think himself esteemed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receive honors with modest reluctance; a measured refusal or slow acceptance makes the donor feel greater esteem and increases the perceived value of the favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know yourself: imitate only what suits your nature and powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man must understand himself and his own powers, and govern himself accordingly, and consider what things he ought to imitate, and what things he ought not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not blindly copy others' manners or talents; assess what suits your temperament and abilities and cultivate those, avoiding affected imitation that falls flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave service of a wicked patron when practicable (except in wartime/adversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Courtier should chance to find himself in the service of one who is vicious and malign, let him depart as soon as he discovers it...provided a gentleman does not leave his patron when at war or in adversity...at any other time he rightly may and ought to leave a service that is like to disgrace him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not continue serving a vicious or dishonourable master when it will disgrace you; remain loyal through adversity/war, but otherwise depart to preserve reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse to obey dishonourable commands
rubrics_metrics.description: In dishonourable things we are not bound to obey any man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obedience to a lord has moral limits; a gentleman is not bound to follow orders that are dishonourable or infamous.
